Biology delivers about 105 boys for every 100 girls. It does this almost everywhere, in almost every era.

On this map a few countries sit above 110. One data map, explained — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ Start with the baseline. Roughly 105 boys per 100 girls at birth is the human norm, and it isn't an accident: boys die at slightly higher rates in infancy and childhood, so the small head start evens out within a few years.

2/ That makes this map unusually easy to read. Most of the world sits in a narrow band around 105. Anything meaningfully above it is not a quirk of biology. It is a decision, taken millions of times over.

3/ The darkest areas are China, Vietnam and Azerbaijan, running around 110 to 112 in recent estimates. India sits above the norm too, though it has been falling. These are the places where girls are missing before birth.

4/ Three things had to line up. A strong preference for sons. Cheap prenatal ultrasound, which spread across Asia in the 1980s. And falling fertility — because when you expect six children, you'll probably get a son anyway.

5/ That last one is the counterintuitive part. Sex selection is not a symptom of poverty or backwardness. It rose alongside smaller families, rising incomes and better healthcare. Fewer chances made each birth higher-stakes.

6/ The Caucasus proves the point. Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia had unremarkable ratios under the USSR, then spiked in the 1990s as fertility collapsed and ultrasound arrived at once. The technology and the arithmetic met.

7/ It is also reversible. South Korea's ratio peaked around 116 in 1990 — worse than anywhere on this map today — and returned to roughly normal within about two decades, as legal enforcement and attitudes toward daughters shifted.

8/ The economist Amartya Sen called the shortfall "missing women" in 1990 and put it in the hundreds of millions across Asia. Those cohorts are now adults, and the map above is what their children's generation looks like.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
